title: Reverse Engineering
tagline: Read compiled programs, find how they work, and build the tools to do it
description: How to understand a program from its compiled form: the ground rules, the tools, the PE file format, reading x64 disassembly of functions, loops, structs and C++ classes, debuggers from the inside, tracing and finding where data is used, patching and hooking programs you build yourself, and writing your own pattern scanner, memory scanner, disassembler and symbol lookup. It ends with reversing a file format, a protocol and a small virtual machine the course provides. Every target is a program you compiled yourself or one the course gives you. It assumes the C++ course and some x64 assembly (the Assembly course or the Game Development course's milestone 7).

milestones.title: Ground Rules, Tools and the PE Format
milestones.blurb: What reverse engineering is and when you may do it, the tools of the trade, and the PE format inside every .exe and .dll: headers, sections, imports, exports and relocations.

lessons.title: What Reverse Engineering Is
lessons.summary: Reverse engineering is working out how a program works from the program itself, without its source. Why people do it - debugging, security, compatibility, preservation, learning - the ground rules about what you may examine, and how this course keeps every target your own.

lessons.title: The Tools of the Trade
lessons.summary: Disassemblers and decompilers for static analysis, debuggers for dynamic analysis, hex editors, PE viewers and system monitors - what each kind of tool does, the free ones worth installing, and a first look at your own program in each.

lessons.title: Inside a PE File
lessons.summary: Every .exe and .dll on Windows is a Portable Executable - a DOS header pointing at the PE headers, a file header, an optional header with the entry point, image base and data directories, and a table of sections. RVAs versus file offsets, and how to convert between them.

lessons.title: Imports, Exports and Relocations
lessons.summary: How a PE says which DLL functions it needs - import descriptors, the import name table and the import address table the loader fills in - how a DLL publishes its own functions in the export directory, and the base relocations that let an image load at any address.

lessons.title: Triage - First Impressions of a Binary
lessons.summary: The first half hour with an unknown program - strings in ASCII and UTF-16, imports and exports, the compiler and runtime it was built with, the PDB path in its debug directory, resources, section entropy and the signs of packing - before reading any code.

milestones.title: Reading Disassembly
milestones.blurb: x64 for readers, recognising functions and their frames, branches, loops and switch tables, structs and arrays in machine code, and what C++ classes, vtables and RTTI look like compiled.

lessons.title: x64 for Readers
lessons.summary: The x64 you need to read compiled code rather than write it - registers and their smaller parts, the handful of instructions that make up most programs, flags and conditional jumps, and the Microsoft x64 calling convention that tells you where every argument and return value is.

lessons.title: Recognising Functions
lessons.summary: Where functions start and end in a binary without symbols - prologues that save registers and reserve stack, epilogues, leaf functions, int3 padding, the .pdata table that lists every function, thunks and tail calls, and following the C runtime's start-up code to main.

lessons.title: Branches, Loops and Switches
lessons.summary: What if, else, && and ||, for and while loops and switch statements compile into, how to read a function as a graph of basic blocks, and the jump tables that big switch statements become.

lessons.title: Data in Machine Code
lessons.summary: Recognising locals, globals, struct members, arrays and strings in disassembly - what the addressing modes reveal, how sizes and signedness show the types, floating point in xmm registers, and rebuilding a struct by collecting every offset the code uses.

lessons.title: C++ in Machine Code
lessons.summary: How C++ features look once compiled by MSVC - this in rcx, constructors that install the vtable pointer, virtual calls through vtable slots, RTTI and the type names it leaves in the binary, name mangling, and the layouts of std::string and std::vector.

projects.title: A control flow graph with loops

milestones.title: Dynamic Analysis
milestones.blurb: How debuggers really work, tracing execution and rebuilding call stacks, finding where a value lives and what changes it, watching a program's behaviour from outside, and comparing runs.

lessons.title: How Debuggers Work
lessons.summary: A debugger is an ordinary program using the Windows debugging API - debug events, software breakpoints made from a single int3 byte, single-stepping with the trap flag, the four hardware breakpoint registers, and first- and second-chance exceptions.

lessons.title: Tracing Execution
lessons.summary: Following what a program actually does - stepping into, over and out, rebuilding the call stack from return addresses, naming addresses as module plus symbol plus offset, conditional and logging breakpoints, and recording traces.

lessons.title: Finding Where Data Lives
lessons.summary: Locating a value in a running program you built - value scanning by narrowing a set of candidate addresses, the types and alignments to search for, then a data breakpoint to find the code that writes it, and working back from that code to the structure and the pointer path that reach it.

lessons.title: Watching Behaviour from Outside
lessons.summary: Learning what a program does without a debugger - Process Monitor's file and registry log and its filters, API Monitor, network captures with Wireshark, Event Tracing for Windows, and Sysmon - and reading their logs systematically.

lessons.title: Comparing Runs
lessons.summary: Differential analysis - snapshot memory before and after an action and diff it, compare which code ran with and without a feature (code coverage diffing), compare files a program wrote, and use time travel debugging to answer questions backwards.

milestones.title: Patching Programs You Build
milestones.blurb: Changing instructions in your own compiled programs, encoding jumps and calls, code caves, hooking functions with trampolines, and byte patterns that keep working after the program is rebuilt.

lessons.title: Patching Instructions
lessons.summary: Changing a compiled program's behaviour by changing its bytes - turning a conditional jump into an unconditional one, inverting a condition, filling instructions with nops - in the file or in memory, on programs you built yourself, and what breaks when you do.

lessons.title: Encoding Jumps and Calls
lessons.summary: How x64 encodes jumps and calls - short and near relative jumps, conditional jumps, relative calls, why the displacement counts from the end of the instruction, the 2 GB limit, and the absolute jumps used when a target is further away.

lessons.title: Code Caves
lessons.summary: When a patch needs more room than the instructions it replaces - finding unused space in a binary, jumping out to it with a detour, running the overwritten instructions there, and jumping back - plus adding a section or allocating memory instead.

lessons.title: Hooking Functions in Your Own Programs
lessons.summary: Redirecting calls to a function so your code runs first - import address table hooks, inline hooks with a trampoline that still calls the original, libraries that do it safely, and using hooks for instrumentation, logging and testing in software you build.

lessons.title: Byte Patterns That Survive Rebuilds
lessons.summary: Every new build moves code around, so fixed addresses break. Byte patterns with wildcards find the same code in any build - which bytes to keep and which to wildcard, keeping a pattern unique, scanning efficiently, and resolving the RIP-relative address inside a match.

milestones.title: Building Your Own Tools
milestones.blurb: How x64 instructions are encoded, a disassembler of your own, reading a process's memory map with documented Windows APIs, symbols and PDB files, and generating byte signatures.

lessons.title: How x64 Instructions Are Encoded
lessons.summary: The layout of an x64 instruction - legacy prefixes, the REX prefix, one to three opcode bytes, the ModRM and SIB bytes that describe operands, displacements and immediates - and how to work out an instruction's length, the first job of any disassembler.

lessons.title: Writing a Disassembler
lessons.summary: From bytes to text - table-driven decoding, naming registers and building memory operands, formatting immediates and branch targets, linear sweep versus recursive descent, telling code from data, and the real libraries (Zydis, Capstone) behind every tool.

lessons.title: Reading a Process's Memory Map
lessons.summary: Seeing a running process the way debuggers do, with documented Windows APIs - opening a process with the right access rights, walking its address space with VirtualQueryEx, understanding states, protections and types, listing its modules, and reading memory safely.

tasks.title: Making sense of a memory map

lessons.title: Symbols and PDB Files
lessons.summary: What a PDB holds, how a binary names its exact PDB through a GUID and age, symbol servers and the path layout they use, public versus private symbols, and turning addresses into names with DbgHelp - including Microsoft's symbols for Windows itself.

lessons.title: Scripting Your Analysis
lessons.summary: Automating the repetitive parts of reverse engineering - scripting Ghidra, IDA and x64dbg, Python with pefile and Capstone for batch work, generating byte signatures automatically, and keeping your findings in a form you can reuse on the next build.

milestones.title: Reversing in Practice
milestones.blurb: A method for unknown programs, reversing a file format and a network protocol from samples, writing up what you found, and a capstone: working out a small virtual machine and its program.

lessons.title: A Method for Unknown Programs
lessons.summary: How to approach a program you know nothing about without getting lost - start from a question, triage, find landmarks, form a hypothesis, test it dynamically, write it down, and know when to stop reading and switch technique.

lessons.title: Reversing a File Format
lessons.summary: Working out an undocumented binary file format from samples - collecting files from controlled changes, magic numbers and versions, lengths and counts, offsets, byte order, strings, checksums and compression - and proving your understanding by writing a parser that reads every sample and a writer the program accepts.

lessons.title: Reversing a Network Protocol
lessons.summary: Working out a custom protocol between a client and a server you run yourself - capturing the traffic, finding how messages are framed in a TCP stream, identifying message types, sequence numbers and fields, handling partial messages, and writing a dissector to decode captures automatically.

lessons.title: Writing It Up
lessons.summary: Turning an analysis into something others can use - the structure of a good report, evidence and reproducibility, annotated databases and headers, clean-room reimplementation, and handling security findings responsibly through coordinated disclosure.

lessons.title: Where to Go Next
lessons.summary: Places to keep practising legally - crackmes and CTF reversing challenges, open-source programs compiled yourself, the FLARE-On challenge, malware analysis training in safe labs - the books and courses worth your time, and what reverse engineering work looks like as a job.
